passage: On Sunday night Valentina filled two pages with rules for the week. If a report is late, then message the owner and log it. If the client emails before nine, then reply after the stand-up. If the budget file changes, then tell the team. Forty-one lines in all. On Wednesday the client rang at eight, two people were out sick, and the budget file broke. She stood at her desk with the notebook open and could not find her place in the pages. Hiroshi leaned in with a loud request about the office move, and she said yes to that, because it was there and he was waiting. By evening the late report was still late. She closed the notebook: forty-one rules, and she had used none.

subtype: Approach: writes so many rules that none can be recalled [Pitfall]
passage:
On Sunday night, Amandeep, the new ward manager at the city hospital's admin block, typed out her weekly plan. It was four pages of if-then rules. If a nurse calls in sick, then check the float list. If the supply order is late, then call the vendor before ten. If a doctor asks for a meeting, then offer Tuesday or Thursday. If... Thirty-eight rules in all.
On Wednesday, everything happened at once. Two staff called in sick, the pharmacy delivery didn't come, and a senior doctor wanted a meeting right now.
Baljeet, her assistant, found her at the desk flipping through the four pages. "Which rule is this?"
"I don't know," she said. "I can't find anything."
By noon she had stopped looking at the pages altogether. She was just answering whoever was loudest, the same as last month.

qa.q: How many rules did Amandeep write?
How was Amandeep feeling when she said she couldn't find anything?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and flustered, with too many rules to remember on a busy day.

qa.q: What would you change first in Amandeep's plan?
qa.a: Cut it down to three or four rules for the most common problems, short enough to remember without looking at the pages.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see the four pages?
qa.a: Baljeet sees they don't help in the moment, since even Amandeep can't find the right rule.

grounding: It shows a young manager making dozens of if-then rules for her week and, on a busy day, remembering none and reacting to the loudest request.

passage:
Dear Jaya,
You asked how the new planning system is going. Honestly? Badly, and I've worked out why.
After that workshop, I wrote if-then rules for everything in my week. If a client emails after six, then reply next morning. If a meeting has no agenda, then decline it. If I get interrupted, then note it and continue. If the report is late, then... I stopped counting at thirty.
Yesterday was the product launch. The phone rang nonstop, three people needed approvals, and a client was angry about an invoice. I didn't remember a single rule. I didn't even open the document. I just answered whatever was loudest, all day, like I always did.
Thirty rules is not a plan, it's a book. Nobody reads a book in a crisis.
I'm going to cut it down. Will tell you how.
Ishita

qa.q: How many rules did Ishita write before stopping counting?
How does Ishita seem to feel about the new system?
qa.a: Ishita seems frustrated and disappointed, admitting it's going badly and the rules were forgotten on the busiest day.

qa.q: What else could Ishita try when cutting the list down?
qa.a: Ishita could keep only three rules for the situations that happen most often, and put them on a sticky note where they can be seen.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jaya may appreciate the honesty and feel curious to hear how the shorter list works.

grounding: It shows a young manager writing so many if-then rules that none can be recalled on a busy day, and reacting to the loudest request instead.
